items.title: On-Device Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech in Google AI Edge Gallery
items.summary: Google AI Edge Gallery now supports on-device, offline Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and Text-to-Speech (TTS) capabilities for building developer-friendly voice applications. Developers can leverage ML Kit for optimized Android performance, or use MediaPipe Tasks and LiteRT for cross-platform open-weight model integration. This local pipeline seamlessly pairs lightweight speech models with on-device small language models like Gemini Nano and Gemma 4 to enable real-time streaming transcription and low-latency synthesis.

items.title: Preview, edit, and collaborate on markdown (.md) files natively in Google Docs and Drive
items.summary: Google Workspace now offers native support for Markdown (.md) files, allowing developers and AI agents to seamlessly collaborate on documentation directly in Google Docs without manual file conversions. This integration preserves native file fidelity for use with Git repositories and developer tools while unlocking standard Docs features like line-level commenting, rendered Drive previews, and tracked version history.

items.title: Integrating TorchTPU into TorchTitan and Optimizing Models for TPU
items.summary: TorchTPU integrates a native torch.device("tpu") backend directly into PyTorch, allowing developers to train large-scale models on Google Cloud TPUs without rewriting code in JAX. The TorchTitan TPU fork enhances this with production-grade scaling primitives like SimpleFSDP, Graph Trainer, and custom Pallas kernels that achieve high Model Flops Utilization (MFU) across dense and MoE architectures. items.summary: A2UI now supports swappable inference formats, introducing A2UI Express which uses up to 3x fewer tokens and cuts latency by compiling compact Python-style syntax into standard A2UI JSON via Agent SDKs. Developers can also use controlled generation with TypeSafe's Jev system-decision models to render known-shape screens in under 300 ms while smaller models stream text. These updates require no changes to frontend renderers or component catalogs, offering flexible performance levers for generative UI development across Python, TypeScript, and Dart.

items.title: Announcing Long-Context Training on TPUs with MaxText Context Parallelism
items.summary: Google Cloud's MaxText framework now supports long-context training up to 14 million tokens on Cloud TPUs by implementing four context-parallel strategies: All-gather, A2A, P2P, and USP. Powered by the Tokamax Splash Attention kernel, these strategies effectively manage attention compute and memory bottlenecks without materializing full key-value sequences in high-bandwidth memory. Developers can adopt these capabilities in MaxText v0.2.4 to achieve high Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) across large-scale model training workflows.

items.summary: A2UI 1.0 is an open protocol for generative UI that enables AI agents to render interactive, native screens across web, mobile, and desktop applications. Developers can leverage open-source renderer SDKs—including React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose—alongside agent SDKs for Python, TypeScript, and Dart. items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. In 6% of encounters, agents act on these comments, with 83% being entirely unprompted by the developer. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.title: What is Pathways? Single-controller training for large models
items.summary: Pathways is a single-controller distributed training system designed to coordinate large-scale model training across multiple accelerator groups by representing computations as a global dataflow graph. Unlike traditional SPMD models like DDP and FSDP that rely on synchronous collectives, Pathways uses asynchronous dispatch and a central scheduler to maximize hardware utilization and prevent deadlocks in complex workloads. By decoupling model definition from physical hardware via virtual devices, developers can efficiently scale complex training architectures and seamlessly handle dynamic workloads like reinforcement learning post-training.

items.title: How Agent Anomaly Detection scores on benchmarks we didn't write

Developers can integrate AAD alongside semantic governance and strict tool limits as part of a defense-in-depth strategy to secure agentic applications.

It merged the files locally, which is a real engineering achievement and the reason I use these things. items.title: 1/7 is a whole number. Your number system just hasn't heard yet.
items.summary: People invented numbers, and the rules you learned in school are one choice. Change a single rule and you get a different number system, just as solid, that mathematicians have used for over a century. In that one, 1 ÷ 7 is a whole number. Grab a calculator. This takes two minutes, and you'll see it happen. 5 × 5 = 25 25 × 25 = 625 625 × 625 = 390625 390625 × 390625 = 152587890625 Look at the end of each answer. It stops changing. …625 shows up and never leaves, then …90625, then …890625. Each step locks in at least one more digit on the right, sometimes several at once. Keep squaring forever and the ending freezes into one endless number that runs off to the left: …918212890625 and here's the weird part: that number is its own square. Check the last few digits yourself: 90625 × 90625 = 8212890625 ← ends in 90625 again There's exactly one other ending like that (besides 0 and 1). It starts from 6: 9376 × 9376 = 87909376 ← ends in 9376 again Now add the two endings: 90625 + 9376 = 100001 Carry that on forever and the twins …918212890625 and …081787109376 add up to exactly 1. For a fintech listing aggregator, one unit might be a normalized listing plus its source URL, publication timestamp, jurisdiction, and an access label. items.title: My SVG Shows Up in the Browser but Not in React. Here's the Checklist I Use
items.summary: You open the .svg file in the browser and it looks perfect. You drop it into a React component and... nothing. No error, or a vague one, and an empty space where the icon should be. The file is almost never the problem. Something between the file and the DOM is. Here is the order I check things in. First, two quick checks. Open the console and look for a React warning. Then inspect the spot where the icon should be: No or element at all? It's the import or the component. The element is there but blank? It's size, paint, or loading. Most bundlers turn import logo from "./logo.svg" into a URL string. Render that as and React gets a string where it expected a component. Vite: add vite-plugin-svgr. In its current major version only imports ending in ?react become components: import Logo from "./logo.svg?react". A plain import stays a URL. For TypeScript, add /// . items.title: Why I chose gRPC for the UI of my POS
items.summary: I spent seven years building a point of sale and adapting it to different customers. Changing the screens was a recurring part of the work. With StillDeep, I wanted to be able to build a different interface for a business while keeping the same engine underneath. That led me to use a public gRPC contract between the UI and the engine. A screen asks for an operation and works with the result. It does not need access to the engine’s internal classes or database. The contract describes the available services, their requests and their responses in Protocol Buffers files. gRPC tooling uses those definitions to generate a client. In C#, that gives me typed requests and responses. When I write a screen, I can see what an operation expects and what it returns. The compiler catches type mismatches while I’m working on the client. It also leaves room for someone to build an interface in another language supported by gRPC. They can generate their client from the same definitions without needing to port the engine to their stack. For me, that is useful when adapting the product to a business. items.title: Tell HN: HN is being scraped for emails to scam
items.summary: I know that many folks here post their personal emails in the Who's for Hire monthly pages and other places, and want to remind you that this public site gets views from folks with ill intent (or their bots/agents) as well. I use unique emails for every site, so I immediately knew that the late AWS payments email sent to my HN email were fake. There were other tells, but I want to remind everyone to be vigilant! HN is public but even social media sites where you supposedly can make your page private I've had some of those emails suddenly have spam sent to as well. Please be safe everyone! My favorite tells that an email is a scam: - Before opening a surprising/suspicious email, hover over the sender name to see the domain the sender came from (don't open the email if it's strange). - _If_ you already opened the email, before clicking any links in the email, hover over them to see the domain that the link sends you to. There are dozens more tips but a full article would be required, and these two will prevent you from falling for nearly all of them. items.title: When a Cached POST Creates Work Twice: Fixing Duplicate Assignments in React and FastAPI
items.summary: A page appeared to stay stuck on the first item opened, while the system quietly created extra work assignments in the background. The bug looked like stale UI state at first. The deeper problem was that a request which changed server state was being treated like a cacheable read. The frontend used a data-fetching query for an endpoint that claimed the next available item. That endpoint did more than retrieve data: it created an assignment and locked the item for the current user. Because the request was cached, revisiting the screen could immediately reuse the first response. A background refetch could then run the POST again, creating another assignment even though the UI continued displaying the original item. There was a second issue: changing only a query-string parameter did not remount the page component. Local state still held the first active item, so the URL and the visible content could disagree. The repair had two coordinated parts. On the backend, the open queue now checks for the caller's oldest in-progress assignment before claiming anything new. items.title: Your .NET License Check Is One `return false` Away From Being Free
items.summary: A hands-on audit you can run against your own binary in 15 minutes - plus the fixes that actually move the needle. You know that scene in every heist movie where the safe has a gorgeous steel door... mounted in a drywall partition? That's most .NET license validation. Strong-looking logic, carefully written guard clauses - sitting in a self-describing binary that hands the attacker a map, a flashlight, and your initials on the keypad. Let's fix that. This post is a practical audit: run it against your own shipped assembly before someone else does. No theory-of-obfuscation lecture - just the checks, the failure modes, and the fixes. I'm using Opaquer (Rustemsoft's free-tier-friendly obfuscator) for the fix side, but the audit part works on any .NET app, protected or not. items.title: Supabase email sign-in and a profiles table for iOS, done safely
items.summary: Almost every iOS app I start needs the same first hour of work: email sign-in, a place to keep per-user data, and a way to make sure users can only touch their own rows. Supabase gives you most of it. The part people get wrong is the profiles table, because the obvious version is also the insecure one. This post walks through the setup I use: the SQL, the Swift, and the three mistakes to avoid. It assumes you know basic SwiftUI and have a free Supabase project. Supabase Auth stores credentials in auth.users. You don't add your own columns there. Instead you create a public.profiles table whose primary key is the auth user's id: create table if not exists public.profiles ( id uuid primary key references auth.users (id) on delete cascade, email text, full_name text, avatar_url text, created_at timestamptz not null default now(), updated_at timestamptz not null default now() ); on delete cascade matters: when the auth user is deleted, the profile goes with it. No orphans. The key in your app is public. Anyone can extract it. So the key is not your security. Row Level Security (RLS) is. alter table public.profiles enable row level security; -- signed-out clients get nothing revoke all

items.summary: Search your app name plus "crack", "cracked" or "free download" on Google, warez and torrent sites, and GitHub. Record those listings by URL and screenshot; do not download from them. This guide is for the developer who published the app, not for someone seeing a Gatekeeper warning. A cracked copy can appear on a warez site, a torrent index or GitHub without showing up in your analytics. Start with a search, not a download. On Google, query your app name plus "crack", "cracked", "free download" or "dmg", and quote the name if it is generic. Repeat those queries on Mac warez sites and torrent indexes, then search GitHub for the app name, your bundle ID, or a distinctive Info.plist string. items.title: Rust Leaves Top 10 in TIOBE Index, Making Room for Go
items.summary: "In November's edition of the TIOBE Index, Rust has dropped out of Top 10," writes I-Programmer, noting that Rust ceded the #10 position to Go. "At the same time, another Google-originated language, Dart, has entered the top 20 ousting Julia after only one month." TIOBE explains Dart's popularity is mainly being driven by Flutter, Google's framework for building cross-platform mobile applications. In fact, Flutter has become one of the major technologies for cross-platform mobile app development. The Dart language itself is not particularly unique, although it incorporates many modern programming language features. Its success is largely driven by the strength of the Flutter ecosystem and the convenience of developing applications for multiple platforms using a single codebase... [In November's ranking] Visual Basic has also lost two places, making room for R and SQL in the Top 10. Further down the ranking, Assembly has re-entered the Top 20. So TIOBE ranks the top 10 languages in November as Python, C, Java, C++, C#, JavaScript, R, SQL, Visual Basic, and Go. items.summary: This week the Linux Foundation's Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF) announced it would broaden its AI security resources, including a new guide to finding and fixing vulnerabilities using AI, "from preparing and sandboxing AI to validating, fixing, and preventing issues." The guide "stresses that AI-generated patches should never be trusted without automated tests and human review. An online course (LFD126) is planned for the coming months." OpenSSF also released the State of AI Impact on Software Security and Cybersecurity 2026 report (supported by OpenSSF, ActiveState and the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation). And it turns out the 2026 report "found a growing gap between the pace of AI-driven software development and organizations' ability to secure the code being produced." 58% of surveyed teams ship code faster than security reviews can keep up, while 60% say AI coding assistants have increased the number of external packages in their codebases. This data underscores the importance of trusted, reliable guidance as AI deployment continues to grow. items.title: Building a read-aloud screen: phrases, tappable words and a finger that drifts
items.summary: Background A lot of what I read is still on paper: letters from the bank, school handouts, a recipe, a library book. I often want to listen to them instead, and I want to follow the words while I listen, so my eyes have something to hold on to. So I built Outloud Reader. You take a photo of a printed page (or open a PDF, or paste text), the app reads it out loud, and the phrase being spoken is highlighted on screen. It runs on iOS and Android, and it can translate a page before reading it. This post is about the reading screen, the part people look at for minutes at a time. It turned out to be the hardest screen in the app to get right. What I wanted from it: the current phrase highlighted, the current sentence easy to find, the rest of the page calm; tap any word to jump the audio there; a "just listen" mode with the text hidden, which you can still peek at; Japanese, Chinese and Thai behaving like any other language. Word-by-word highlighting, like karaoke. It is still in the code as an option, but it was exhausting to watch. items.title: I built a free Mac dictation app that never sends your voice to a server
items.summary: A few months ago my wrists started aching by mid-afternoon. I type for a living, most days for nine to twelve hours, and by evening I was closing the laptop instead of answering one more email. I tried the voice to text apps people recommend. A couple of them are good. Every one I tried wanted a monthly subscription and sent my voice to a server before the text came back, and I've written enough software to know that audio can sit on somebody else's disk for as long as they like. So I built my own, over a few weekends that turned into a few months. I wanted to see whether small open models could do the whole job on a laptop people already own. The result is Purr, a free, open-source menu bar app for macOS. You hold Right Option, talk and let go, and the words get typed into whatever text field has focus. It doesn't need an account, and nothing it hears leaves your Mac. Once the models have downloaded, it works offline. What it does Dictation is the main thing. If you'd rather see words appear while you talk, Smart Typing types as you speak instead of waiting for the key to come up. Voice Edit works on text you've already written. items.summary: Today Fadely is live on Product Hunt 🚀 👉 https://www.producthunt.com/posts/fadely My brother-in-law flies constantly. One day he found his passport photo buried among hundreds of old downloads on his phone. First relief, then worry: what if his phone gets stolen? We all do this. We save a boarding pass, a ticket or an ID copy "just for a trip", and it stays on our phone for years. Fadely is a vault for documents you only need for a while: ✈️ Add boarding passes, tickets, a passport copy 📅 Pick an expiry date 🔔 Get a reminder 24 hours and 1 hour before, and extend it by 48 hours from the notification if your trip runs late 🔒 When the date comes, the vault is gone for good Each vault is encrypted with AES-256 and its own key, stored in the iOS Keychain When a vault expires, its key is deleted, so the files become unreadable noise If iOS skips the background task, the vault is always destroyed before it can be opened again The countdown widget uses a pre-built timeline, so it updates at the exact expiry without opening the app, and it only holds emoji and dates, never documents or keys No accounts, no cloud, no backups, no analytics. items.summary: NSCollectionView 有 4 種排版： 排版 1：1 個 Cell（1） 排版 2：2 個 Cell（2） 排版 3：3 個 Cell（1 + 2） 排版 4：5 個 Cell（2 + 3） 畫面目前有 5 個 Cell，使用排版 4（2 + 3） 使用者點擊第一排右側的 Close Button Cell 被刪除，排版依剩餘 Cell 數量重新切換 使用者立即點擊原本的位置 該位置明明有 Close Button，卻沒有觸發刪除 停頓一小段時間後，又可以正常點擊 使用 deleteItems(at:) 刪除 Cell，沒有呼叫 reloadData 只有排版改變時，才會發生點擊後沒有刪除的情況 把 deleteItems(at:) 改成每次都 reloadData，反而每次刪除後都會發生 prepareForReuse 沒有遺漏重置資料 刪除 Cell 時，main thread 上沒有耗時的工作 多次嘗試沒有結果後，改從滑鼠事件本身調查。我請 AI 加入更完整的 Debug Log，觀察： mouseDown 事件實際由哪個 Button 接收 mouseUp 事件的流向 NSEvent.clickCount 的變化 滑鼠目前位置透過 Hit Test 找到的 View 把過濾後的 Log 貼給 AI，能快速分析出情況，節省時間。 快速連續點擊時，Log 出現了一個很特別的現象：clickCount 持續增加，但接收 mouseDown 的 Button 始終是同一個實例。 Click 1 clickCount = 1 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button A Click 2 clickCount = 2 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button B Click 3 clickCount = 3 mouseDown self = 0xbb545ed00 (Button A) hitTest = Button B 這代表： 第一下點擊時，接收事件的是 Button A。 Cell 刪除並重新排版後，滑鼠下方已經變成 Button B（Hit Test 的結果）。 但後續點擊的 mouseDown，仍然由 Button A 接收。 畫面上滑鼠下方的 Button，和實際收到滑鼠事件的 Button，並不是同一個。 TODO（發文前請確認）：目前只觀察到現象，尚未確認 AppKit 為何在連續點擊時沿用舊的接收者，也沒驗證「停頓後恢復」是否與系統雙擊間隔有關。若有實測或文件佐證，請補在這裡；沒有的話，這段維持「觀察到的現象」即可。 在 Button 的 mouseDown 中判斷事件是否真的落在自己身上

items.title: Building a Privacy-First Desktop OCR & Translation Pipeline for macOS: Deep Dive into Apple Vision Framework
items.summary: As developers and researchers, our desktop screens display our most sensitive intellectual property: uncommitted proprietary code, confidential game crash logs, private API keys, and draft academic papers. Yet, many popular desktop translation utilities take an alarming architectural shortcut: they capture your screen and ship the entire raw PNG/JPEG image directly to cloud-hosted computer vision APIs. In this technical breakdown, we explore how to build a Privacy-First Desktop OCR & Translation Architecture on macOS. By leveraging Apple's native Vision Framework and ScreenCaptureKit, we ensure that image frames never leave the user's local machine, while only sanitized textual tokens cross the network boundary. When an application asks for macOS Screen Recording permissions, it gains access to every pixel rendered on the display. items.title: I shipped a VPN app on iOS, Mac, Android and Windows without writing a VPN protocol
items.summary: I build mobile apps for a living, mostly on iOS. This year I shipped a VPN called Privalune on iPhone, iPad, Mac, Android and Windows. I did it alone, and the only reason that was possible is one decision I made early: I would not write or bundle a VPN protocol. Every platform I target already ships an IKEv2 client. So the apps are remote controls. They hand the operating system a server and a login, and the OS runs the tunnel. This post covers how that works on each platform, what the backend looks like, and where the approach hurts. The numbers None of those codebases contains cryptography or packet handling. iOS and Mac: NEVPNManager On Apple platforms the system VPN is NEVPNManager, the "Personal VPN" API. You fill in an IKEv2 profile, save it, and ask the system to start it. iOS shows its own permission prompt the first time. The part I like most is on-demand rules. items.title: The git worktrees your coding agents leave behind, and how to clean them up
items.summary: Claude Code, Cursor and Codex run in git worktrees so several agents can work at once. Each worktree is a full checkout with its own node_modules and build output, and they pile up quietly. One Claude Code user found 27 forgotten worktrees using 80 GB (issue 63087). 61 Codex worktrees of a Rails app took about 100 GB (issue 35383). Claude Code: .claude/worktrees/ inside each repository (older versions used ~/.claude-worktrees) Cursor: ~/.cursor/worktrees/ Codex: ~/.codex/worktrees/, on a detached HEAD rather than a branch git worktree list # inside a repository du -sh .claude/worktrees/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h # inside each repository du -sh ~/.cursor/worktrees/*/* ~/.codex/worktrees/* 2>/dev/null | sort -h git -C status --short # prints nothing if nothing is uncommitted git -C status --short --ignored # .env and other ignored files you'd lose git log --oneline main.. # prints nothing if the branch is merged Squash merges leave the commits out of main, so ask GitHub instead: gh pr list --head --state merged --json headRefOid, and check it matches git rev-parse . git worktree remove Skip --force: without it, git refuses when there's uncommitted work, which is the point. items.title: Eliminating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference with Integer-Only Arithmetic (15 minute read)
items.summary: A floating-point number stores a fixed number of significant digits and a separate exponent. When two numbers with very different exponents are added, the small one has to be shifted to line up with the big one, and the digits that fall off on the end are gone. That means that (a+b)+c is not always equal to a+(b+c). This post looks at what happens when integer addition, which is exact, is used.

items.title: Handing over humanity (22 minute read)
items.summary: Some AI experts believe that once we achieve superintelligence, humans will be permanently disempowered, and we shall all be ruled by an AI god. This might not be such a desirable outcome, as humans have a natural desire for freedom. The arrangement will probably not work, as keeping power responsive to human needs has required checks developed over centuries, sustained by repeated feedback from the real world and correction, and there's no reason to keep that equilibrium stable once humans have surrendered all control. Humans have the ability now to steer the technology in a way that will not lead to a complete replacement of human judgment.

items.title: What objective is reasoning solving? (12 minute read)
items.summary: Reasoning is pathfinding in token space. There are many paths from the problem to a correct answer, and the model traverses each of them with each sample. A path is not guaranteed to converge to the correct answer - it's only in aggregate, over the distribution of paths, do we get a high probability of success. RL training directly raises the success probability. The gains credited to 'thinking longer' come from the search paid for during training rather than at inference.

items.title: Two Kinds of Test-Time Scaling (28 minute read)
items.summary: Test-time scaling trades compute for performance at test time. There are two types of test-time scaling: one allows researchers to trade more compute for more performance per task, but only up to the maximum quantity of per-task compute used during training; and the other lets researchers trade more compute for more performance per task, and lets them do so up to quantities of compute and performance that never occurred during training. Scaling methods that permit the latter change will have a larger impact than test-time scaling considered simply. This essay describes how this may impact the world.

It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.
